full_judgment:
ABM Khairul Haque J: This Rule, under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, was issued at the instance of the accused-petitioner calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the proceeding of the Special Tribunal Case No. 22 of 1994 arising out of Miscellaneous Case No. 345 of 1994 pending in the Court of Special Tribunal No.1, Panchagarh, should not be quashed. 

 2. The fact of the case, in brief, is that the accused-petitioner is a friend of the complainant and used to visit his house often and on the pretext of his friendship, on the night following 2-6-1993, the accused petitioner abducted his wife, After futile attempts to trace his wife, the complainant opposite party No. 1 filed the instant case before the learned Magistrate, First Class Panchagarh, on 7-6-1994, being Miscellaneous Case No. 345 of 1994. The learned Magistrate on receipt of the petition of complaint examined the complainant under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and forwarded his petition of complaint to the concerned police station for investigation. The officer in-charge Panchagarh police station, in due compliance of the order of the learned Magistrate submitted his investigation report on 4-7-1994 (Annexure-B to the petition). In his report he stated that after investigation he found prima facie evidence about the allegations made by the complainant in his petition of complaint against the accused-opposite party. The learned Magistrate on receipt of the investigation report from the officer-in-charge, Panchagarh police station by his order dated 7-7-1994 found the case to be triable under section 27 of the Special Powers Act and forwarded the case records to the Court of Special Tribunal. Panchagarh on receipt of the records from the Magistrate First Class, Panchagarh, The Special Tribunal No. 1 Panchagarh, took cognizance of the offence under the Special Powers Act, and issued warrant of arrest against the accused- petitioner by an Order dated 16-7-1994 in Special Tribunal Case No. 22 of 1994. Being aggrieved the accused petitioner obtained the present Rule under section 561A of the CrPC. 

 4. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that in the instant case the Magistrate on receipt of the petition of complaint. (Annexure A to the petition) from the complainant, though investigated by a police officer sent the case records to the Special Tribunal for trial who illegally took cognizance of the offence against the accused-petitioner because the case was initially started on petition of complaint by a complainant before the learned Magistrate but without a police report in writing as envisaged under sub-section (I) of section 27 of the Special Powers Act and, as such violative of the said provision and without jurisdiction on a plain reading of sub-section (1) of section 27 of the Special Powers Act 1974 it appears that the Special Tribunal constituted of an offence triable under the said Act on a report in writing made by a police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector, The words "report in writing made by a police officer" was not explained in the Special Powers Act but section 29 of the Special Powers Act provides that the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure so far only as they are not inconsistent with the provision of the Act. shall apply to the proceedings of a Special Tribunal and such Special Tribunal shall have all powers conferred by the Code on a Court of Session exercising original jurisdiction. The effect of this provision is that a Special Tribunal is clothed with all the powers of a Sessions Judge, save and except those which are inconsistent with the provisions of the Special Powers Act. In the instant case, the learned Magistrate on receipt of the complaint examined the complainant under section 200 of the Code. Thereafter directed an investigation by the police presumably under sub-section (I) of section 202 of the Code. Section 202 sub-section (I) of the Code reads as follows: 

 "202-(I) Any Magistrate on receipt of a complaint of an offence of which he is authorised to take cognizance or which has been transferred is him under section 192, may, if he thinks fit, for reasons to be recorded in writing, postpone the issue of process for compelling the attendance of the person complained against, and either inquire into the case himself, or if he is a Magistrate other than a Magistrate of the third class, direct an inquiry or investigation to be made by any Magistrate subordinate to him. or by a police officer or by such other person as he thinks, fit, for the purpose of ascertaining the truth or falsehood of the complaint." 

 5. On a reading of section 202 of the Code it appears that under sub-section (I) a Magistrate, on receipt of the complaint, may take cognizance of any offence on the basis of the allegations made by the complainant on solemn affirmation by him before the Magistrate or he may have the matter enquired or investigates into either by a Magistrate or by a police officer or by any other person as the case may be and thereafter may proceed in accordance with the situation that arises in the case. In this case on receipt of a complaint, the Magistrate examined the complainant but in order to ascertain truth of falsehood of the complaint sent the petition of complaint to the concerned police station for investigation. On receipt of the report submitted by the officer-in-charge of the concerned police station and on consideration of the deposition of the complainant on oath the learned Magistrate came to the conclusion that the offence as alleged in the petition of complaint. was prima facie established for trial by the Special Tribunal under the provision of the Special Powers Act. As such, he rightly' forwarded the case records to the Special Tribunal, Panchagarh and on consideration of the report submitted by the officer-in-charge. Debiganj Police Station the Special Tribunal No.1 Panchagarh took cognizance of the offence against the accused petitioner presumably under sub-section (1) of section 27 of the Special Powers Act. As such, the submission of the learned Advocate that the Special Tribunal took cognizance of the offence without any pol ice report is not correct. The report dated 4-7-1994 (Annexure-B to the petition) submitted by the officer-in-charge, police station Debiganj is a report in writing made by a police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector as' envisaged under sub- section (1) of section 27 of the Special Powers Act. 

 6. Syed Ziaul Karim, the learned Advocate, next submits that it is true that a Magistrate, on receipt of a petition of complaint, may direct an investigation only if he is himself authorised to take cognizance of the offence or which has been transferred to him under section 192 of the Code but in the instant case, the allegations as made out in the petition of complaint were not triable by a Magistrate but by the Special Tribunal, as such, he was not even authorised to send the petition of complaint to the officer-in-charge of the concerned police station for investigation as envisaged under section 202 of the Code. According to the learned Advocate, this power to direct investigation is available only to those Magistrates who can take cognizance of the offence as alleged but if the allegations, as in this case, is triable by a Special Tribunal he cannot direct such an investigation. Since the order of investigation was without jurisdiction the learned Advocate submits that since the Magistrate sent the case records to the Special Tribunal on the basis of such investigating report the taking of cognizance by the Special Tribunal, even on the basis of a police report, is also without jurisdiction. The argument of the learned Advocate though attractive but is fallacious. When a petition of complaint is filed before a Magistrate, it cannot be said at that stage as to whether cognizance of the offence can at all be taken if and so under what provision of law. Under such circumstances, the Magistrate is required to follow the procedure laid down in chapter XVI of the Code. In the instant case, on receipt of the petition of complaint the learned Magistrate examined the complainant on oath under section 200 of the Code and thereafter in exercise of his powers under section 202 of the Code directed an investigation by the police. Only on receipt of the report by the police he came to the conclusion that the offence as alleged in the petition of complaint is triable by the Special Tribunal under the Special Powers Act, as such, the learned Magistrate in exercise of his powers under section 190 of the Code. rightly sent the case to the Special Tribunal Panchagarh, for disposal. In this connection, it should be borne in mind that on receipt of the petition of complaint the learned Magistrate at the initial stage proceeded under chapter XVI and Chapter XV of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Only when he came to the conclusion about the nature of allegation he sent the case records to the appropriate Court for disposal under the appropriate law. The submission of the learned Advocate that the learned Magistrate can direct an investigation only in those cases where he himself can take cognizance is not correct. An enquiry or an investigation can also be directed by the Magistrate under section 202 of the Code is, order to ascertain the nature of the allegation and to decide whether cognizance of the offence should be taken because till then he is in seisin of the case. 

 7. In the instant case the complainant in his petition of complaint alleged that he had been to the police station for lodging the information of abduction of his wife but without getting any response from there he filed the petition of complaint before the Magistrate. In such circumstances, it is wrong to say that simply because the case was started on a petition of complaint, the Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act would have no jurisdiction to try the case, if it is otherwise triable under the Act. On this point if we accept the argument of the learned lawyer for the petitioner, the position will be that a person who goes to the police station to lodge first information report if denied that relief, he will have no other relief by way of filing a petition of complaint before a Magistrate, under such circumstance such a person will be without any relief which cannot be conceived of. Under the provision of Special Powers Act, no petition of complaint can directly be filed before a Special Tribunal. The Special Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to try all such cases which come within the ambit of the Special Powers Act, started on the basis of a petition of complaint, provided of course, there is a police report in writing by a police officer not below the rank of a Sub-Inspector as is envisaged in sub-section (1) of section 27 of the Act. 

 8. In this case there was no illegality or irregularity on the part of the learned Magistrate in taking steps under sections 200/202/190 of the Code on receipt of the petition of complaint and hence he sent the records of the case along with' the police report to the Special Tribunal. The Special Tribunal also rightly took cognizance of the offence under section 27(1) (2) of the Special Powers Act. Under Karim' Advocate, has got no substance and the petition under section 561A of the Code of Criminal procedure is misconceive and is liable to be discharged. 

 As the case is an old one, the Special Tribunal No. 1 Panchagarh is directed to dispose of the case as expeditiously as possible preferably within six months from the date of receipt of the judgment of this Court.
